section_summary: This section records debate over Japan’s postwar deconcentration program after the SCAP Deconcentration Review Board announced four principles for applying the Deconcentration Law. Despatches, press coverage, and State Department memoranda assess whether those principles weaken company reorganizations and how the United States should proceed in the Far Eastern Commission. The section also reviews the progress of zaibatsu dissolution and proposed revisions to Japan’s Anti-Monopoly Law.

subfiles.title: Policy recommendations on excessive concentrations of economic power
subfiles.about: The paper recommends divestiture and measures to prevent renewed concentrations of economic power in Japan.
subfiles.summary: It proposes removing controlling individuals from positions that could obstruct reform, compensating them for divested assets, and distributing securities widely. It allows public acquisition or regulation where competition is impractical, protects United Nations nationals’ interests, and sets suggested 1949 deadlines. Further recommendations address credit, monopolistic practices, patent and corporate law, taxation, small businesses, and conflicts between government personnel and private enterprises.

subfiles.title: Telegram transmitting SCAP’s deconcentration press statement
subfiles.about: The telegram transmits a press statement announcing four principles for administering Japan’s Deconcentration Law.
subfiles.summary: The principles require a prima facie case of restricted competition, reject unrelated businesses or a voluntary plan as sufficient grounds for an order, and tie any remedy to the grounds for designation. The statement says basic policy has not changed and identifies participants in the Review Board’s meeting with the Holding Company Liquidation Commission.

subfiles.title: Policy Announced by Deconcentration Review Board
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, Office of the Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The despatch argues that the Review Board’s four principles substantially relax application of the Deconcentration Law.
subfiles.summary: Sebald reports that the new prima facie requirement may be difficult to satisfy in Japan’s controlled economy and could release many firms from designation. He discusses the suspended Nippon Soda reorganization, favorable reactions from business and the Japanese press, and expectations of revisions to the Anti-Monopoly Law.

subfiles.title: SCAP’s Deconcentration Review Board and Holding Company Liquidation Commission Hold Meeting
subfiles.about: The release sets out the four principles announced after the Review Board’s first meeting with the Holding Company Liquidation Commission.
subfiles.summary: It states that the principles preserve existing deconcentration policy while clarifying when companies may be designated and what remedies may be ordered. It lists the officials attending the meeting.

subfiles.title: 4 New Principles Change HCLC Plan
subfiles.about: The article predicts that the new principles will alter reviews of designated companies.
subfiles.summary: It reports that the HCLC will re-examine 275 firms and reconsider the proposed division of Nihon Soda.

subfiles.title: The Deconcentration Review Board
subfiles.about: The editorial welcomes the Review Board’s principles as reassurance about Japan’s deconcentration program.
subfiles.summary: It argues that the principles should ease fears that deconcentration would harm production or economic recovery.

subfiles.title: Operation of Deconcentration Law Vital
subfiles.about: The editorial supports prompt, more flexible deconcentration alongside broader enterprise reconstruction.
subfiles.summary: It welcomes the four principles and argues against mechanically dividing large firms. It also calls for revaluing fixed assets, resolving new-account deficits, and raising capital for equipment.

subfiles.title: Urgent Antimonopoly Law Revisions Impending
subfiles.from: Tokyo Shimbun; translated by J. Ide
subfiles.about: The editorial urges relaxation of restrictions on international agreements and stock acquisition.
subfiles.summary: It argues that revisions would ease foreign investment and trade while retaining fair competition.

subfiles.title: Central News Agency report on deconcentration
subfiles.about: The telegram relays a Tokyo news report claiming that the Deconcentration Law may be abandoned.
subfiles.summary: The report interprets the four principles as sharply narrowing deconcentration and predicts that most large corporations will remain intact.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Tokyo despatch No. 619
subfiles.about: The memorandum summarizes the Review Board’s four principles and reactions to them.
subfiles.summary: It notes Welsh’s concern that the new test may release many designated companies, describes favorable Japanese business reactions, and identifies Nippon Soda as a test case.

subfiles.title: Proposed Course of Action on Japanese Industrial Deconcentration
subfiles.about: The memorandum assesses the policy significance of the four principles and recommends a United States course in the Far Eastern Commission.
subfiles.summary: It finds some liberalization but cautions that the principles alone do not prove the program has been abandoned. It recommends withdrawing a delayed telegram seeking the Review Board’s terms of reference and avoiding a new United States deconcentration paper in the Far Eastern Commission.

subfiles.title: Draft telegram requesting deconcentration reports
subfiles.about: The draft requests progress reports, Review Board terms of reference, and information on cases and procedures.
subfiles.summary: It seeks information for deciding how to proceed in the Far Eastern Commission.

subfiles.title: Telegram reporting securities sales and control-association closures
subfiles.about: The telegram gives figures from SCAP’s July summary of nonmilitary activities.
subfiles.summary: It reports share sales worth 1.77 billion yen and 980 cumulative control-association closures.

subfiles.title: Repeated telegram on securities sales and control-association closures
subfiles.about: This copy repeats the figures for securities sales and control-association closures.
subfiles.summary: It reports the same SCAP figures as the preceding telegram.

subfiles.title: Proposed Course of Action on Japanese Industrial Deconcentration
subfiles.about: The memorandum recommends withdrawing a pending telegram and avoiding a new Far Eastern Commission policy proposal.
subfiles.summary: Fearey argues that sending the delayed telegram could be misread by SCAP and that a policy presentation might provoke controversy. He suggests stating that no new commission decision is necessary while continuing to supply requested information.

subfiles.title: FEC 230
subfiles.about: The memorandum sets conditions for withdrawing the United States deconcentration proposal from the Far Eastern Commission.
subfiles.summary: It identifies risks for continued implementation, banking reform, major company cases, and securities disposal. It proposes a public reaffirmation of United States aims, policy advice to SCAP, and renewed review of securities sales.

subfiles.title: File charge slip for September 30 document
subfiles.about: The form records a file charge for a document dated September 30.
subfiles.summary: Administrative charge record for file 894.602/9-3048.

subfiles.title: Handwritten note on deconcentration policy differences
subfiles.about: Saltzman calls for discussion of differing departmental views on further deconcentration action.
subfiles.summary: He asks to discuss the Economic Affairs view and reach an agreed answer.

subfiles.title: Present Status of the Zaibatsu Program in Japan
subfiles.about: The memorandum reviews legislation, implementation, and unresolved issues in Japan’s zaibatsu program.
subfiles.summary: It describes liquidation and antitrust laws, company designations, and enforcement against restraints of trade. It finds limited progress on secondary corporate ties, oversized firms, and especially banking concentration. Securities sales remain incomplete, raising questions about market effects, ownership, and the pace of liquidation.

subfiles.title: Revision of Anti-Monopoly Law
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The despatch compares successive Japanese proposals to revise the Anti-Monopoly Law.
subfiles.summary: Sebald reports that a later Cabinet proposal would ease restrictions on international contracts, stock and debenture holdings, concurrent directorships, and mergers more than an earlier Fair Trade Commission draft. He attributes the shift partly to the Review Board’s intervention and expects substantial revisions to reach the Diet.

subfiles.title: Extracts from Law No. 54 of 1947
subfiles.from: Office of the Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The enclosure reproduces articles of the existing Anti-Monopoly Law relevant to proposed revisions.
subfiles.summary: The extracts cover concerted restraints, international agreements, holding companies, intercorporate stock and debenture holdings, joint officers, individual stockholdings, mergers, business transfers, and evasion. They provide the legal baseline for the accompanying despatch’s comparison of amendment proposals.

subfiles.title: Private Interests Lobby on Monopoly Law Revision
subfiles.from: Nihon Keizai; translated by T. Mitsuhashi
subfiles.about: The article describes business lobbying for Anti-Monopoly Law revisions to facilitate foreign capital and trade.
subfiles.summary: It reports disagreements between government and business groups and lists proposed changes concerning international agreements, corporate share and debenture ownership, concurrent posts, mergers, and the law’s coverage thresholds.
